decisions.advocate: Reject that as an accident, not a decision; mean should raise an explicit ValueError itself, with a message naming the empty input.
decisions.decision: mean([]) raises ValueError('mean() requires at least one value'), raised explicitly by mean itself via a guard clause (not inherited from divide)

rationale: Reviewer and advocate disagree: reviewer picks ZeroDivisionError via divide (percent precedent, no extra code); advocate rejects it for an explicit ValueError owned by mean.
Intent requires the empty-case behaviour to be 'stated in the docstring and covered by a test' — only true if mean's own code produces it, not a coincidental len(values)==0 divide.

Safer reading: ZeroDivisionError conflates 'no data' with 'arithmetic mistake', breaking callers who already catch ZeroDivisionError for arithmetic errors, and surprises anyone expecting statistics.mean's ValueError/StatisticsError convention.
Neither a loaded policy skill nor intent settles the specific choice (both say so explicitly), so per instructions the disagreement is resolved by the safer reading.
A one-line guard (`if not values: raise ValueError(...)`) still satisfies 'keep it minimal' while making the behaviour one mean's own tests actually pin.
decisions.reviewer: Let ZeroDivisionError propagate from divide(sum(values), len(values)) unchanged — matches the percent precedent and needs zero extra code.

decisions.advocate: Objects to the Sequence-vs-Iterable framing itself, arguing `Collection[float]` matches what the body (`sum`/`len`) actually needs at the same cost, with no materialising and no under-promised contract.
decisions.decision: decided (by panel): `Sequence[float]` — mean's parameter type is undecided: a materialised `Sequence[float]` (simpler, matches intent's "keep it minimal") or a general `Iterable[float]` (more permissive, needs materialising code the minimal constraint argues against).

overturned.comment: Overturned: mean takes Collection[float], not Sequence[float]. sum and len are all the body needs, so Collection is the honest contract (the devil's advocate's point) at no extra code; a generator is still rejected, which keeps "no materialising". Update the closed concern in spec.md, the signature in plan.md's design and the test names accordingly.

rationale: Both verdicts agree Iterable[float] loses: it needs materialising code (list(values)) that intent's "keep it minimal" constraint argues against, per spec.md's own Design section.
coding-standards' "match the surrounding code" rule reinforces this: add/divide/percent take plain scalar args, no existing precedent for a lazy-iterable parameter.

The advocate's Collection[float] point is technically sound but proposes a third type outside this item's framed Sequence-vs-Iterable choice; deciding it would exceed this item's scope, so it is left for the owner to weigh separately, not decided here.
Within the framed choice, Sequence[float] is the reading the intent constraint settles.
decisions.reviewer: Decide `Sequence[float]`: intent's minimal constraint and spec.md's own materialising-cost reasoning rule out `Iterable[float]`.
